evidence: Opened the primary source: raw files from raw.githubusercontent.com at branch `dev` (default branch; last push 2026-02-04, 14 commits, 6 stars), downloaded to /var/folders/mf/9v804k_57lq30kwtlr7468xr0000gn/T/driftcheck/ and read in full. Files read line-by-line: src/config.rs (all 343 lines — contains the three system prompts as Rust consts, lines 7-39), src/llm.rs (all 262), src/analyzer.rs (all 151), src/search.rs (all 312), src/main.rs (all 274), src/git.rs (all 121), src/output.rs (all 32), src/tui/app.rs (lines 30-180, 181-316, 625-693 — contains the repair prompt at 662-668), src/tui/mod.rs (16), .pre-commit-hooks.yaml (8), .github/workflows/ci.yml (45), README.md (all 460, read as three numbered slices). There are no separate instruction/rule .md files in this repo — the "rule files" ARE the Rust string constants in src/config.rs and src/tui/app.rs; I read those constants verbatim. Also ran grep over all sources to test claims (git-log context, unused config keys, test count).
whatItIs: A ~1.2k-line Rust CLI that installs a git pre-push hook (src/git.rs:9-16, `exec driftcheck hook`). Pipeline (src/analyzer.rs:34-121): take `git diff @{u}..HEAD` (src/git.rs:19-40); LLM call #1 turns the diff into a JSON array of ripgrep patterns (prompt at src/config.rs:34-36); ripgrep those patterns over doc globs with `-C 3`, dedupe by file:line, merge chunks within 5 lines, truncate to 8000 tokens (src/search.rs:114-267, src/analyzer.rs:124-151); LLM call #2 receives `## Code Diff` + `## Documentation Excerpts` and returns a JSON array of issues (src/llm.rs:198-206). Decision rule is entirely prompt-encoded (src/config.rs:7-32), user-overridable via `[prompts] analysis` in .driftcheck.toml. On a finding: TTY → a ratatui TUI where `a` sends the whole doc file to a third LLM call that rewrites it (src/tui/app.rs:633-693) and writes in place with no diff preview and no commit; non-TTY → print to stderr and `process::exit(1)`, blocking the push (src/main.rs:263-271).
measures: Nothing. The repo ships four unit tests, all of them for parsing ripgrep's `file:line:content` output format (src/search.rs:269-312); CI runs only build/test/clippy/fmt (.github/workflows/ci.yml:35-45). There is no eval set, no labelled drift corpus, no precision/recall or false-positive number anywhere — despite "Conservative by default — Only flags clear, factual errors to minimize false positives" being the headline claim (README.md:15, 135-139, 419-433). The central claim is asserted in prose inside a prompt ("Be conservative. When in doubt, think twice. False positives waste developer time." — src/config.rs:23) and never tested.

practices.practice: In the judging prompt, give the model a closed whitelist of reportable defect types and an explicit DO-NOT-REPORT blacklist, instead of a quality rubric. driftcheck's whitelist is exactly three: docs state something now factually wrong; a doc code example would now fail; a documented signature/parameter/return type now differs. Its blacklist is five: stylistic improvements, vague-but-not-wrong, potential clarifications, anything still technically accurate, anything already fixed. For terse's audit this maps onto the `lie` failure class: the reader model should be told what NOT to raise, so it stops emitting style notes.
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted only. The rationale sentence is itself in the prompt (src/config.rs:23); the repo contains no measurement of whether the blacklist reduces false positives.
practices.costAndCollision: ~15 lines added to the audit prompt. Mild collision with 'no noise' — it is prompt text, not output text, so it costs tokens, not reader time. It is the un-preachy shape of an instruction: enumerated conditions, no adjectives.

practices.practice: Force every finding into a fixed JSON schema whose fields include a verbatim excerpt of the offending text plus file and approximate line: {file, line, description, doc_excerpt, suggested_fix}. Requiring the model to quote the exact wrong sentence back is a cheap hallucination check — a finding that cannot quote its own target is discardable.
practices.locus: src/config.rs:27-32 (schema block of the prompt); src/llm.rs:252-261 (RawIssue deser, `line` and `doc_excerpt` default so a malformed answer still parses)
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted. No measurement of how often the excerpt fails to match the file; notably nothing in the code verifies that `doc_excerpt` actually appears in the named file — the check is offered to the human reader, not enforced.
practices.costAndCollision: Near zero for terse's audit, which already reports per-question failures. Adds one required field. Enforcing the quote mechanically (string-match the excerpt against the file) is the improvement driftcheck left on the table.

practices.practice: Derive the search terms from the code, then grep the docs for them — and enumerate the term categories in the prompt so the model does not free-associate: function names, class names, API endpoints, CLI flags, config keys, error messages. Zero hits for a term means the docs never name the thing. For terse this is a mechanical findability probe that needs no model to score.
practices.locus: src/config.rs:34-36 (DEFAULT_SEARCH_QUERIES_PROMPT, the category list is line 35); src/search.rs:114-143 (rg -C 3 over doc globs)
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted. The category list is plausible and concrete but unmeasured; retrieval quality is never evaluated.
practices.costAndCollision: Cheap: one grep pass. Complements terse's `findability` failure class with a zero-LLM signal, so it reduces rather than adds noise.

practices.practice: Split retrieval from judgement into two separate model calls, and cache the first keyed on the input hash. The retrieval call is cheap, deterministic-ish (temperature 0.1) and reusable; only the judgement call sees the assembled context.
practices.locus: src/analyzer.rs:52-107 (the three-step pipeline); src/analyzer.rs:55-76 (cache lookup on the diff); src/llm.rs:76 (temperature 0.1 for all calls)
practices.costAndCollision: Structural; terse's audit already fans one model per question, so this mostly confirms the shape.

practices.practice: Put a hard context budget on the retrieved excerpts and state the merge rules: dedupe by file:line, merge chunks in the same file within 5 lines with a '...' marker, then fill up to the budget. Take the shape; do NOT take driftcheck's ranking — it sorts by chunk size and its own comment admits this is a placeholder for relevance.
practices.locus: src/analyzer.rs:124-151 (truncate_to_budget; the admission is the comment at line 130: sort 'for now, just by size'); src/search.rs:246-267 (merge_adjacent_chunks)
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted, and self-flagged as provisional in a source comment. The 4-chars-per-token estimate (analyzer.rs:126) is a guess.
practices.costAndCollision: Low. Relevant only if terse's audit ever feeds excerpts rather than whole .md files.

practices.practice: Write the repair prompt as a whole-file rewrite bounded by four rules: output only the fixed file content with no explanation; make minimal changes, only what is necessary; preserve all formatting, whitespace and structure; if something is missing, add it in the appropriate place. Feed it the issue (file, line, problem, suggested fix) plus the complete current file.
practices.locus: src/tui/app.rs:662-668 (system prompt) and 670-690 (user prompt layout: ## Issue / ## Suggested Fix / ## Current File Content)
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted. No before/after measurement; the fix is written straight to disk (src/tui/app.rs:645-647) with no verification that it resolved the issue.
practices.costAndCollision: Directly comparable to terse's revise repair pass — same whole-file-rewrite shape, four rules, no rubric. Cheap to adopt as a wording reference; collides with nothing.

practices.practice: If a check ever blocks, the blocking message must advertise its own bypass in the same breath, and the tool must ship multiple off-switches: an env var, a config flag for 'proceed on tool error', and a subcommand to disable. driftcheck prints `git push --no-verify` in the failure text itself.
practices.locus: src/main.rs:267-270 (the blocking message); src/config.rs:291-299 (DRIFTCHECK_DISABLED=1); src/main.rs:235-240 and 249-255 (allow_push_on_error); README.md:435-441
practices.costAndCollision: Collides head-on with terse's already-rejected 'CI gates'. Record as a conditional rule — IF terse ever gates anything, it must print the bypass — never as a reason to gate.

practices.practice: Cautionary, not to adopt: do not write an instruction that inverts the rule stated one sentence earlier. driftcheck's prompt says to skip issues in recently-modified docs, then says 'Only flag issues for files that were updated in recent commits' — which commands the opposite. A rule the model can satisfy by doing either thing measures nothing.
practices.evidenceForIt: Proven by reading the two lines together; the second sentence is missing a negation ('were NOT updated').
practices.costAndCollision: Free. Worth a line in terse's own audit checklist for instruction files: check each rule against its neighbours for inversion.

weaknesses:
Four defects, three of them proven by grep, and they matter more to terse than the tool does.

1. PROVEN — the judging prompt consumes context that is never supplied. src/config.rs:19 says "check the git log provided" and :21 says "Review the recent commits section." The only `git` invocations in the codebase are `git diff` (src/git.rs:29-32) and `rev-parse @{u}` (src/git.rs:44-46); the user message is built at src/llm.rs:198-201 from the diff and doc chunks only. `grep -rn "commit" src/*.rs` returns exactly two hits, both inside that prompt string. The model is told to consult a section that does not exist — it can only invent or ignore it. This is the single most transferable lesson here for terse: an instruction file that references absent context is a defect class an audit should hunt for.

2. PROVEN — the README documents behaviour the code does not have, in three places. README.md:14, 125-128, 138 and 433 all advertise "Checks recent commits to avoid flagging already-fixed issues" (see defect 1). README.md:190 documents `auto_apply = false`; `auto_apply` and `show_diff_preview` are declared at src/config.rs:102-104 and defaulted at :214-215 and read nowhere else in the codebase. README.md:417 states that a missing config blocks the push; src/main.rs:216-222 returns Ok(()) on ConfigNotFound, so the push proceeds. `prompts.suggestions` (src/config.rs:38-39) is dead too — only `.analysis` and `.search_queries` are ever read (src/llm.rs:146, 203). A documentation-drift detector whose own docs have drifted, in the exact categories it claims to catch.

3. PROVEN — zero evaluation. Four unit tests, all on ripgrep output parsing (src/search.rs:269-312). The "conservative, minimises false positives" claim has no number behind it anywhere.

4. HYPOTHESIS — the interactive path silently un-gates. src/main.rs:263-271: non-TTY prints and exits 1; TTY hands off to the TUI, which returns Ok(()) whenever the user presses Enter with nothing pending (src/tui/app.rs:289-312, 130-132), including when every issue was skipped with `s` (:282-287). So marking all findings "skip" lets the push through with exit 0; only `q`/Esc aborts (:134-138). Mechanism read from source; not executed, so I label it hypothesis. Related: pressing `a` rewrites the doc file on disk mid-push without staging or committing it, so the pushed commit still contains the stale text and the fix lands as an uncommitted working-tree change (src/tui/app.rs:645-647; README.md:353 admits "review all changes with `git diff` before committing").

Scope limits for terse: this tool measures drift between a diff and doc excerpts. It says nothing about whether a document can be read, understood, or navigated — no reader model, no questions, no profile, no comprehension score. It is adjacent to terse's audit only in sharing the premise that code is ground truth and docs are the accused. Adoption is minimal (6 stars, single author, 14 commits, last push 2026-02-04), so none of its prompt wording carries field validation.
method: driftcheck encodes its method as three prompt constants plus a fixed pipeline. Drift is decided by a single LLM call, at temperature 0.1, that sees a `git diff` of `@{u}..HEAD` alongside ripgrep excerpts of the docs, under a prompt (src/config.rs:7-32) that defines drift narrowly: report ONLY when the docs explicitly state something now factually wrong because of the change, when a doc code example would now fail, or when a documented signature/parameter/return type now differs — and never report style, vagueness, possible improvements, still-accurate text, or anything the recent commits appear to have fixed. It closes with "Be conservative... False positives waste developer time" and demands an empty array when nothing clears the bar. Retrieval comes first and is also an LLM call: the diff is turned into a JSON array of ripgrep patterns, with the prompt naming the categories to look for (function names, class names, API endpoints, CLI flags, config keys, error messages); those patterns are grepped with three lines of context across the configured doc globs in parallel, deduped by file:line, merged when within five lines, and packed to an 8000-token budget. Output is a JSON array of {file, line, description, doc_excerpt, suggested_fix}, where doc_excerpt must be the exact wrong text; the parser tolerates prose around the array and treats "no issues"/"no documentation" as empty. With findings in hand, a TTY opens a TUI where each issue can be applied — a third LLM call rewrites the entire doc file under four rules (output only the content, minimal changes, preserve all formatting, add missing material in the right place) and overwrites the file in place — or skipped; pressing Enter with nothing pending exits zero and the push proceeds, while q/Esc aborts it. Without a TTY, the issues print to stderr and the process exits 1, blocking the push, with the message itself naming `git push --no-verify` as the bypass. The whole decision rule is user-replaceable from .driftcheck.toml, which is the tool's real stance: the rules are configuration, not code.
